claim: ArhGAP44 is predominantly expressed in the brain compared to other organs in rats.
source: western blot analysis showed expression of ArhGAP44 in the brain while being below detection level in all other tested organs (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A and immunoblotting results

claim: Within the brain, ArhGAP44 shows increased protein levels in the frontal cortex and olfactory bulb.
source: Immunoblotting directed against ArhGAP44 showed increased protein levels in the frontal cortex and olfactory bulb (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B

claim: ArhGAP44 protein levels increase during neuronal development in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with the micro-array data, ArhGAP44 protein levels increased with time (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis at DIV3, DIV10, and DIV17 shown in Figure 1C

claim: Convoluted membrane sections (nodes) are observed along dendrites at DIV10.
source: High magnification micrographs further showed convoluted membrane sections (i.e., convoluted nodes) along the dendrite at DIV10 that may reflect such local regions of high curvature (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1D

claim: Overexpression of ArhGAP44 causes a significant reduction in the density of dendritic filopodia at DIV12.
source: Compared to control cells, overexpression of ArhGAP44 caused a significant reduction in the density of dendritic filopodia at DIV12 (Figure 1E, dark blue)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia density shown in Figure 1E

claim: Expression of the ArhGAP44(R291M) mutant reduces but does not abolish GTP hydrolysis of Rac1.
source: Consistent with partial activity, expression of the ArhGAP44(R291M) mutant reduced but did not abolish GTP hydrolysis of the small GTPase Rac1 (Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activation assay data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Knockdown of ArhGAP44 augments the density of dendritic filopodia.
source: Markedly, knockdown of ArhGAP44 augmented the density of dendritic filopodia (Figure 1G, yellow)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia density after siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 1G

claim: Both siRNA pools directed against ArhGAP44 significantly reduced protein levels of ArhGAP44.
source: Both siRNAs were effective since protein levels of ArhGAP44 were significantly reduced in cells co-transfected with either one of the siRNA pools directed against ArhGAP44 (Figure 1H)
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1H

claim: ArhGAP44 primarily limits filopodia formation with little effect on the stabilization of existing filopodia.
source: Together, these results argue that ArhGAP44 primarily limits filopodia formation with little effect on the stabilization of existing filopodia
evidence: Inferred from time-lapse imaging data showing changes in dynamic but not static protrusions

claim: Expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) reduces the formation of transient protrusions compared to control.
source: Compared to control, neither knockdown of ArhGAP44 nor expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) showed significant changes in the density of static protrusions that persisted longer than 10 min (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Video 1) In contrast, expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) reduced (Figure 2B, blue and Video 2)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Knockdown of ArhGAP44 increases the formation of dynamic protrusions.
source: whereas knockdown of ArhGAP44 increased (Figure 2B, yellow and Video 3 and Video 4) the formation of dynamic protrusions
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The majority (83% ± 7%) of de novo protrusions extend from node-like structures.
source: Intriguingly, we find that the majority (83% ± 7%) of de novo protrusions extended from such node-like structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Video 6)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The GAP domain of ArhGAP44 inhibits GTPase activity of both Rac and Cdc42.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Richnau and Aspenstrom, 2001), we find that the GAP domain of ArhGAP44 inhibits GTPase activity of Rac and Cdc42 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: Supported by GTPase pull-down assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and cited literature

claim: Overexpression of wild-type Rac1 but not Cdc42 phenocopies protrusion density observed upon knockdown of ArhGAP44.
source: We find that overexpression of wild-type Rac (human Rac1) but not Cdc42 phenocopied protrusion density (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B

claim: Co-expression of Rac1 with ArhGAP44(R291M) reverses the observed decrease in the frequency of protrusion formation caused by expression of ArhGAP44(R291M).
source: Although the resulting protrusions were shorter than control filopodia, co-expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) together with Rac1 reversed the observed decrease in the frequency of protrusion formation and node formation caused by expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) (Figure 2E,F purple and Video 11)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: Endogenous ArhGAP44 is absent from the nucleus and present in patches along dendrites.
source: We found ArhGAP44 to be absent from the nucleus and present in patches along dendrites (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2A

claim: Fluorescently tagged ArhGAP44 was excluded from the nucleus, distributed uniformly through the cytosol, and formed distinct ArhGAP44 patches along dendrites.
source: Like the endogenous protein, fluorescently tagged ArhGAP44 was excluded from the nucleus, distributed uniformly through the cytosol, and formed distinct ArhGAP44 patches along dendrites (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C)
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C

claim: Full-length protein and the isolated N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 both enriched in patches along dendritic arbors.
source: Full-length protein and the isolated N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 both enriched in patches along dendritic arbors, while deletion of the amino-terminal amphipathic helix (ΔN-BAR), a critical sequence motif for binding and stabilization of curved membranes (Peter et al., 2004), showed no enrichment over a cytosolic reference (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B and cited literature on N-BAR domain function

claim: None of the ArhGAP44 constructs enriched in extended filopodia.
source: Intriguingly, none of the ArhGAP44 constructs enriched in extended filopodia (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Time-lapse imaging showed that filopodia often emerged from ArhGAP44 patches.
source: Time-lapse imaging showed that filopodia often emerged from ArhGAP44 patches (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Formation of actin patches precedes extension of exploratory filopodia.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Lau et al., 1999; Spillane et al., 2012), ratio-imaging of the filamentous actin marker f-tractin (Johnson and Schell, 2009) to a cytosolic reference showed formation of actin patches that preceded extension of exploratory filopodia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 12)
evidence: Supported by ratio-imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited literature

claim: 89% ± 6% of all filopodia emerge from actin patches.
source: This was the case in 89% ± 6% of all filopodia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Actin intensity in nodes is significantly higher compared to adjacent dendritic sections.
source: Consistent with a role of actin in node-formation, we find that actin intensity in nodes was significantly higher compared to adjacent dendritic sections (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by correlative light and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: F-tractin shows significant enrichment in ArhGAP44 patches.
source: We then expressed f-tractin together with the isolated N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 and found significant enrichment of f-tractin in ArhGAP44 patches (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 enriched in dendritic actin-patches by 80% ± 8% compared to adjacent dendritic regions.
source: Consistently, the N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 enriched in dendritic actin-patches by 80% ± 8% compared to adjacent dendritic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B

claim: NMHC-2B shows significant enrichment in ArhGAP44 patches.
source: To test for Myosin II-dependent contractile forces in ArhGAP44 patches, we co-expressed the isolated N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 and non-muscle Myosin Heavy Chain IIB (NMHC-2B) and found a significant enrichment of NMHC-2B in ArhGAP44 patches (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Phosphorylated myosin light chain (pMLC), a marker for active Myosin II, shows increased staining in dendritic actin patches.
source: Consistently, we find increased staining for the phosphorylated form of myosin light chain (pMLC), a marker for active Myosin II (Tan et al., 1992), in dendritic actin patches (Figure 4D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D and cited literature on pMLC as a marker

claim: Inhibition of actin integrity or myosin-dependent actin contraction leads to a significant reduction of ArhGAP44 concentration in actin patches.
source: Notably, both treatments led to a significant reduction of ArhGAP44 concentration in actin patches (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B after drug treatment

claim: ArhGAP44 is enriched at inward plasma membrane deformation created by retracting lamellipodia.
source: Notably, we find ArhGAP44 to be also enriched at inward plasma membrane deformation created by retracting lamellipodia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 13)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: ArhGAP44 is enriched in response to membrane bending by artificial nanocone structures.
source: as well as in response to membrane bending by artificial nanocone structures (Figure 5—figure supplements 3,4; and Videos 14,15)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4

claim: Inward membrane deformation is sufficient for binding of ArhGAP44 to the plasma membrane.
source: arguing that inward membrane deformation is sufficient for binding of ArhGAP44 to the plasma membrane
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing ArhGAP44 enrichment at artificially induced membrane deformations

claim: The N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 is enriched at the end of dendrites (dendritic tips).
source: We find the N-BAR domain enriched at the end of dendrites (dendritic tips; Figure 5—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: The N-BAR domain of ArhGAP44 is enriched in spine-shaped dendritic protrusions.
source: as well as in spine-shaped dendritic protrusions (Figure 5—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6

claim: Knockdown of ArhGAP44 in aged neurons facilitates re-emergence of exploratory dendritic protrusions.
source: Knockdown of ArhGAP44 in aged neurons facilitates re-emergence of exploratory dendritic protrusions (Figure 5—figure supplement 7)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7

claim: Recruitment of ArhGAP44 to actin patches is mediated by Myosin II-dependent contraction of membrane-associated actin cables.
source: Our study shows that recruitment of ArhGAP44 to actin patches, which seed exploratory filopodia along dendritic branches, is mediated by Myosin II-dependent contraction of membrane-associated actin cables
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing drug-induced reduction of ArhGAP44 enrichment and co-localization with myosin markers

claim: Actin patches serve as precursors for the formation of filopodia in axons.
source: These actin patches have been shown to serve as precursors for the formation of filopodia in axons (Lau et al., 1999; Spillane et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Actin patches serve as precursors for the formation of filopodia in dendrites.
source: and dendrites (Korobova and Svitkina, 2010)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Individual actin filaments within the actin cortex form bundles prior to filopodia elongation in non-neuronal cells.
source: Studies in non-neuronal cells showed that individual actin filaments within the actin cortex form bundles prior to filopodia elongation (Svitkina et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Filopodial actin bundles are embedded in the underlying dendritic actin meshwork.
source: Consistently, electron micrographs of neurons showed that these filopodial actin bundles are embedded in the underlying dendritic actin meshwork (Korobova and Svitkina, 2010)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Once enough actin filaments are bundled to generate the force required to protrude the PM, the resulting outward membrane deformation triggers recruitment of actin bundling/Cdc42 activating proteins.
source: It has been proposed that once enough actin filaments are bundled to generate the force required to protrude the PM, the resulting outward membrane deformation triggers recruitment of actin bundling/Cdc42 activating proteins, which then further increase the polymerization rate within the extending filopodia (Krugmann et al., 2001; Disanza et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Myosin II-dependent contraction of individual actin filaments within actin patches provides structural integrity to counter the force generated by the extending filopodia.
source: Given the localization of Myosin II in actin patches (Figure 4D), it is reasonable to conjecture that Myosin II-dependent contraction of individual actin filaments within actin patches provides structural integrity to counter the force generated by the extending filopodia
evidence: Inferred from the localization of Myosin II in actin patches

claim: Myosin II-dependent contraction exerts an inward directed pull force that curves the PM inward which triggers increased recruitment of ArhGAP44.
source: However, considering that individual actin filaments within a bundle are oriented with the barbed end to the PM, Myosin II-dependent contraction also exerts an inward directed pull forces that curve the PM inward which triggers increased recruitment of ArhGAP44
evidence: Inferred from the orientation of actin filaments and the observed recruitment of ArhGAP44

claim: The highly convoluted membrane topography associated with actin patches reflects Myosin II-dependent contraction of membrane-associated actin cables.
source: We propose that the highly convoluted membrane topography associated with actin patches (Figure 4A) reflect such Myosin II-dependent contraction of membrane-associated actin cables, at which ArhGAP44 becomes enriched in a curvature-dependent manner
evidence: Inferred from the observed membrane topography and ArhGAP44 enrichment

claim: Inward membrane deformation is sufficient for ArhGAP44 and N-BAR domain recruitment.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we find not only that inward membrane deformation is sufficient for ArhGAP44 and N-BAR domain recruitment (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4)
evidence: Supported by experiments with artificial nanocone structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4

claim: Deletion of ArhGAP44 curvature-sensitivity prevents ArhGAP44 enrichment.
source: but that deletion of ArhGAP44 curvature-sensitivity (Figure 3A,B) or reducing action-myosin-dependent contractile forces (Figure 5A) both prevented ArhGAP44 enrichment
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A, 3B, and 5A

claim: Reducing acto-myosin-dependent contractile forces prevents ArhGAP44 enrichment.
source: but that deletion of ArhGAP44 curvature-sensitivity (Figure 3A,B) or reducing action-myosin-dependent contractile forces (Figure 5A) both prevented ArhGAP44 enrichment
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: A likely function of local ArhGAP44 at actin patches is to suppress GTPase-mediated local actin polymerization.
source: We show that ArhGAP44 can hydrolize the small GTPase Rac and Cdc42 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). Thus, a likely function of local ArhGAP44 at actin patches is to suppress GTPase-mediated local actin polymerization
evidence: Inferred from the GAP activity of ArhGAP44 and its localization to actin patches

claim: ArhGAP44 is limiting Rac-dependent formation of actin patches, which provide the structural integrity required for filopodia to protrude outwards.
source: We propose that ArhGAP44 is limiting Rac-dependent formation of actin patches, which provide the structural integrity required for filopodia to protrude outwards (Figure 6)
evidence: Inferred from the GAP activity of ArhGAP44 and the observed effects on filopodia formation

claim: Dynamic rearrangements within actin patches rely on Rac activity in neurons.
source: This is consistent with previous reports in neurons, showing that dynamic rearrangements within actin patches relies on Rac activity (Andersen et al., 2005; Spillane et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Elevated Rac levels increase filopodia dynamics.
source: and that elevated Rac levels increase filopodia dynamics (Luo et al., 1996; Nakayama et al., 2000; Zhang and Macara, 2006; Cheadle and Biederer, 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Rac1 is localized at actin patches.
source: In support of this notion, we find Rac1 localized at actin patches (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Artificial decrease of ArhGAP44 concentration at actin patches by knockdown increases the number of exploratory filopodia.
source: and show that artificial decrease of ArhGAP44 concentration at actin patches either by reducing overall ArhGAP44 levels by knockdown (Figure 1F) or by preventing ArhGAP44-recruitment to actin patches via inhibition of acto-myosin contraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, see also [Ryu et al., 2006; Hodges et al., 2011]) both increased the number of exploratory filopodia
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and cited literature

claim: Artificial decrease of ArhGAP44 concentration at actin patches by preventing ArhGAP44-recruitment via inhibition of acto-myosin contraction increases the number of exploratory filopodia.
source: and show that artificial decrease of ArhGAP44 concentration at actin patches either by reducing overall ArhGAP44 levels by knockdown (Figure 1F) or by preventing ArhGAP44-recruitment to actin patches via inhibition of acto-myosin contraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, see also [Ryu et al., 2006; Hodges et al., 2011]) both increased the number of exploratory filopodia
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and cited literature

claim: Cdc42 acts as an activator of Irsp53, promoting IRSp53-dependent enrichment and clustering of VASP and other factors to drive actin assembly in elongating filopodia.
source: Cdc42 acts as an activator of Irsp53 (Kast et al., 2014), promoting IRSp53-dependent enrichment and clustering of VASP and other factors to drive actin assembly in elongating filopodia (Disanza et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Knockdown of Cdc42 substantially reduces filopodia formation in neurons.
source: Consistently, knockdown of Cdc42 substantially reduces filopodia formation in neurons (Garvalov et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Overexpression of Cdc42 is not sufficient to initiate filopodia formation in neurons.
source: Intriguingly, overexpression of Cdc42 is not sufficient to initiate filopodia formation in neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, see also [Hotulainen et al., 2009])
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and cited literature

claim: Overexpression of Cdc42 is not sufficient to initiate filopodia formation in other cell lines.
source: or in other cell lines (Kast et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Elongation of filopodia is a combinatorial process requiring multiple factors.
source: This has led to the hypothesis that elongation of filopodia is a combinatorial process requiring multiple factors (Kast et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Signal integration at actin patches controls the decision of filopodia elongation.
source: We propose that signal integration at actin patches controls this decision of filopodia elongation
evidence: Inferred from the observed localization and function of ArhGAP44 at actin patches

claim: Actin-patch formation occurs before filopodia elongation.
source: Considering that actin-patch formation occurs before filopodia elongation, this argues for a 2-step process where Rac1-induced patch formation (and ArhGAP44-dependent regulation thereof) precedes Cdc42-induced filopodia elongation (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data showing temporal sequence

claim: Rac1-induced patch formation (and ArhGAP44-dependent regulation thereof) precedes Cdc42-induced filopodia elongation.
source: this argues for a 2-step process where Rac1-induced patch formation (and ArhGAP44-dependent regulation thereof) precedes Cdc42-induced filopodia elongation (Figure 6)
evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of events and the dual specificity of ArhGAP44

claim: Since ArhGAP44 shows dual specificity for Rac1 and Cdc42, both steps (patch formation and filopodia elongation) will be limited by recruitment by ArhGAP44 to actin patches.
source: However, since ArhGAP44 shows dual specificity for Rac1 and Cdc42, both steps will be limited by recruitment by ArhGAP44 to actin patches
evidence: Inferred from the dual GAP activity of ArhGAP44 and its localization

claim: ArhGAP44 mediates a localized negative feedback that becomes upregulated as neurons mature to reduce the frequency with which neurons initiate new exploratory filopodia.
source: Taken together, we propose that ArhGAP44 mediates a localized negative feedback that becomes upregulated as neurons mature to reduce the frequency with which neurons initiate new exploratory filopodia
evidence: Inferred from the observed increase in ArhGAP44 expression with neuronal maturation and its inhibitory effect on filopodia formation

claim: Acto-myosin initiated PM deformation is a ubiquitous process.
source: Considering that acto-myosin initiated PM deformation is a ubiquitous process and that a high number of curvature-sensing proteins are known to modify actin dynamics
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cellular processes

claim: A high number of curvature-sensing proteins are known to modify actin dynamics.
source: Considering that acto-myosin initiated PM deformation is a ubiquitous process and that a high number of curvature-sensing proteins are known to modify actin dynamics
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about curvature-sensing proteins

claim: The local feedback mechanism for ArhGAP44 likely exemplifies a more general principle for receptor-independent signaling whereby signal transduction is initiated by the transient recruitment of regulatory proteins to actin- and force-dependent nanoscale PM indentations.
source: this suggests that the local feedback mechanism for ArhGAP44 described in our study likely exemplifies a more general principle for receptor-independent signaling whereby signal transduction is initiated by the transient recruitment of regulatory proteins to actin- and force-dependent nanoscale PM indentations
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observed mechanism and general principles of cell biology

claim: 286 genes were identified in a NCBI data-search that were previously associated either directly or indirectly with actin reorganization.
source: To identify new regulators of exploratory dendritic filopodia formation, we performed a literature search and identified 286 genes that were previously associated either directly or indirectly with actin reorganization
evidence: Based on literature search methodology described in Materials and methods

claim: 89 of the 286 genes were found to be expressed predominantly in neuronal tissues.
source: We then clustered these genes according to expression pattern using published microarray data and found 89 of the 286 genes to be expressed predominantly in neuronal tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 'Materials and methods' and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Based on clustering analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: ArhGAP44 (also known as Rich2 or Nadrin2) is a membrane-curvature-sensing GTPase Activating Protein (GAP) selective for the small Rho GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42.
source: Among the five actin regulators with the highest brain vs spinal cord ratio, we found ArhGAP44 (also known as Rich2 or Nadrin2), a membrane-curvature-sensing GTPase Activating Protein (GAP) selective for the small Rho GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42 (Richnau and Aspenstrom, 2001)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: ArhGAP44 has been associated with the maintenance of apical microvilli in polarized epithelial cells.
source: In previous studies, ArhGAP44 has been associated with the maintenance of apical microvilli in polarized epithelial cells as well as postsynaptic maturation and vesicle release (Rollason et al., 2009; Nahm et al., 2010; Raynaud et al., 2013, 2014)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: ArhGAP44 has been associated with postsynaptic maturation and vesicle release.
source: In previous studies, ArhGAP44 has been associated with the maintenance of apical microvilli in polarized epithelial cells as well as postsynaptic maturation and vesicle release (Rollason et al., 2009; Nahm et al., 2010; Raynaud et al., 2013, 2014)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Rho GTPases play a role during filopodia formation.
source: Considering the role of Rho GTPases during filopodia formation (Krugmann et al., 2001), we decided to further investigate the role of ArhGAP44 in developing neurons
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: The same expression pattern of ArhGAP44 was found in sagittal brain sections stained against ArhGAP44.
source: The same expression pattern was found in sagittal brain sections stained against ArhGAP44 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: ArhGAP44 is among the genes with the highest adult-to-fetal ratio in the brain.
source: We then explored the expression of ArhGAP44 in the brain during development and found ArhGAP44 among the genes with the highest adult-to-fetal ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 2 and 'Materials and methods')
evidence: Based on microarray data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Prolonged expression of ArhGAP44 increased the fraction of cells forming varicosities.
source: Prolonged expression increased the fraction of cells forming varicosities, likely due to increased RhoGAP activity associated with elevated ArhGAP44 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Expression of the ArhGAP44(R291M) mutant showed a milder loss in filopodia density compared to wild-type ArhGAP44.
source: Consistent with partial activity, expression of the ArhGAP44(R291M) mutant reduced but did not abolish GTP hydrolysis of the small GTPase Rac1 (Figure 1F), showed a milder loss in filopodia density (Figure 1E, light blue)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: Expression of the ArhGAP44(R291M) mutant delayed the onset of varicosity formation.
source: and delayed the onset of varicosity formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Control experiments using a second siRNA pool directed against a different region of ArhGAP44 mRNA confirmed the phenotype of increased filopodia density.
source: Control experiments using a second siRNA pool directed against a different region of ArhGAP44 mRNA confirmed the phenotype, thus showing that siRNA knockdown and overexpression of ArhGAP44 have opposing effects
evidence: Supported by experimental data using two independent siRNA pools

claim: siRNA knockdown and overexpression of ArhGAP44 have opposing effects on filopodia density.
source: Control experiments using a second siRNA pool directed against a different region of ArhGAP44 mRNA confirmed the phenotype, thus showing that siRNA knockdown and overexpression of ArhGAP44 have opposing effects
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing knockdown and overexpression

claim: Dendritic filopodia frequently extend, reorient, and collapse.
source: As dendritic filopodia frequently extend, reorient, and collapse (Ziv and Smith, 1996), filopodia density reflects the product of de novo formation frequency and stabilization rate
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Filopodia density reflects the product of de novo formation frequency and stabilization rate.
source: As dendritic filopodia frequently extend, reorient, and collapse (Ziv and Smith, 1996), filopodia density reflects the product of de novo formation frequency and stabilization rate
evidence: Inferred from the dynamic nature of filopodia

claim: Neither knockdown of ArhGAP44 nor expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) showed significant changes in the density of static protrusions that persisted longer than 10 min.
source: Compared to control, neither knockdown of ArhGAP44 nor expression of ArhGAP44(R291M) showed significant changes in the density of static protrusions that persisted longer than 10 min (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Video 1)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Most newly formed protrusions were short-lived.
source: Most of these newly formed protrusions were short-lived, while stabilization of extending protrusions or collapse of previously static protrusions was observed only infrequently (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Stabilization of extending protrusions or collapse of previously static protrusions was observed only infrequently.
source: Most of these newly formed protrusions were short-lived, while stabilization of extending protrusions or collapse of previously static protrusions was observed only infrequently (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: For both overexpression and knockdown of ArhGAP44, an increase in the number of transiently formed nodes along dendritic arbors was observed.
source: For both, overexpression and knockdown of ArhGAP44, we further observed an increase in the number of transiently formed nodes along dendritic arbors (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Videos 2–5)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Nodal structures likely represent nascent filopodia sites, where filopodia formation is either initiated or aborted.
source: We thus consider these nodal structures to represent nascent filopodia sites, where filopodia formation is either initiated or aborted
evidence: Inferred from the observation that filopodia emerge from nodes

claim: Nodal structures likely correlate with the convoluted nodes along dendrites seen in electron microscopy studies.
source: Given their spacing and their presence at the same time in culture, they likely correlate with the convoluted nodes along dendrites seen in electron microscopy studies (Figure 1D)
evidence: Inferred from the spatial and temporal correspondence between fluorescence and EM observations

claim: Overexpression of wild-type Rac1 but not Cdc42 phenocopies protrusion kinetics observed upon knockdown of ArhGAP44.
source: We find that overexpression of wild-type Rac (human Rac1) but not Cdc42 phenocopied protrusion density (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B) as well as protrusion kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C and Videos 7–10) observed upon knockdown of ArhGAP44
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B and 5C

claim: Rac1 overexpression increased protrusion dynamics and node formation similar to knockdown of ArhGAP44.
source: Similar to knockdown of ArhGAP44, Rac1 overexpression increased protrusion dynamics and node formation (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5D and Videos 7,8)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D-F

claim: Rac activity is associated with increased actin patch formation and filopodia dynamics in axons.
source: These observations are consistent with previous work showing Rac activity associated with increased actin patch formation and filopodia dynamics in axons (Spillane et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: Rac activity is associated with increased actin patch formation and filopodia dynamics in dendrites.
source: and dendrites (Korobova and Svitkina, 2010; Cheadle and Biederer, 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature

claim: ArhGAP44 might act by inhibiting Rac to limit initiation of exploratory filopodia formation.
source: We thus considered that ArhGAP44 might act by inhibiting Rac to limit initiation of exploratory filopodia formation
